Hi everyone,

This thread has been a great help and I appreciate the responsiveness and help of this community in general!

I have a question about stacking for my data. I have camera data from the summers of two years that differ in length of survey (July - October 2018,  June - October 2019). I currently have weeks set as my observation period. Thus I have 17 observations for my first year and 22 observations for my second year.

In stacking as I understand it, I would then have each site*year as a separate "site". My detection histories (y data) would then be of different lengths as the first year has fewer observations than the second year (2018 [43 x 17], 2019 [48 x 22]) such as this:

"site 1"   y11 y21 y31
"site 2"   y12 y22 y32 y42 y52

What is the appropriate way of dealing with this?

I would imagine you would fill the spaces with NAs. At that point is it better to:
           1) align the detection histories by time so that each observation has a fixed point in season (e.g. July 1st 2018 and July 1st 2019 share the same observation column)
               "site 1"  NA   NA   y11  y21   y31
               "site 2"  y12  y22  y32  y42   y52
OR
          2) align the first dates of survey so that each observation has a relative point in each season (e.g. July 1st 2018 and June 1st 2019 share the same observation column)
             "site 1"  y11  y21  y31  NA  NA
             "site 2" y12  y22   y32  y42  y52

Thanks so much for taking a look at this and setting me right!

Best,

Edward

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Is model averaging bad?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

On of the issues highlighted by Cade 2015 (Cade, B. S. 2015. Model averaging and muddled multimodel inferences. Ecology 96:2370-2382.) is related to using strongly correlated variables in your models. Regardless of the approach used, it is always a good idea to avoid including correlated variables in a given model, to choose the scales of the variables wisely, and avoid overparameterizing the models (these issues are present in Cade's examples). This is not specific to model averaging. Another issue highlighted by Cade 2015 is the problem of using relative importance of variables: these are not very informative and should not be used to make inferences and I totally agree.

Regarding averaging (beta) coefficients, there are some known issues with the natural average method (Burnham and Anderson 2002, top of p. 152; modavg( ) in AICcmodavg) that involves recomputing the model selection table for only the models that include the explanatory variable of interest. If you model average beta coefficients for a variable that appears only in models with little or no support, then you will likely overestimate the effect of the variable. So, at best, using the natural average should be limited to variables that appear in the top-ranked models. As a result, it is not recommended to systematically model-average beta coefficients for all variables in your model set.

The second method of model averaging betas is using the shrinkage estimator (Burnham and Anderson 2002, bottom of p. 152; modavgShrink( ) in AICcmodavg), which retains all models in the computations. When using this method, a variable not appearing in a model will be assigned a beta of 0 for the model. As a result, if models that do not include the variable of interest have strong support, the model-averaged beta will be shrunk towards zero. Overall, this provides a more balanced way of assessing the effect of the variable, because all models are used. When using this method, each variable should appear in the same number of models and a given variable should have the same interpretation across all models (this can be an issue in the presence of quadratic or other interaction terms).

Model-averaging predictions is the original reason for doing model averaging across an entire model set and is the "gold standard". One way of assessing if there are issues with the natural average method is to compare the model-averaged beta coefficient against the plot of model-averaged predictions across the variable of interest. If the model-averaged predictions show a null pattern and your natural average beta estimate is saying something different, that is evidence that you shouldn't be using the natural average for your inferences.

An alternative to model-averaging beta coefficients, is to focus on effect sizes (i.e., differences between groups; modavgEffect( ) in AICcmodavg), which brings the problem to model-averaging differences between predictions across the entire model set (Burnham et al. 2011: AIC model selection and multimodel inference in behaviorial ecology: some background, observations and comparisons. Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 65:23-25.

Regardless of the model-averaging method used, some found that the variance estimates used to compute confidence intervals do not perform nominally with small sample sizes and suggest an alternative estimator involving tail areas (Turek and Fletcher 2012: Model-averaged Wald confidence intervals. Computational Statistics and Data Analysis 56:2809-2815.).

Hope it helps,

Marc

messages.body_plain:
It's not a problem. It's just telling you that it's converting your data from one data type (character, or letters) to another (factor, which is when the computer represents each category with a number. So every entry for "GRASS" becomes a 1 and every entry for "MONT" becomes a 2.). This is a necessary step before fitting a model.

Here's more on data types in R: https://www.tutorialspoint.com/r/r_data_types.htm#:~:text=green%22%20%22yellow%22-,Factors,or%20character%20or%20Boolean%20etc.

messages.subject: Re: occFormulas Fdesign values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tristan,

Unless you have an absolutely gigantic dataset, you are unlikely to get useful estimates from unmarked for a 9-species model in which you try to estimate all the possible species interactions up to the 9th order. I would suggest constraining the model in some way. You could consider a smaller subset of species (2-4, maybe 5 tends to work well). Alternatively, in many cases only the pairwise interactions between species are of biological interest. If that's the case, you can set the argument "maxOrder=2" when you run occuMulti, which will require a smaller number of formulas (9 first-order + 36 possible pairwise = 45). Even with that simplification you may have trouble given the number of parameters that must be estimated.

To actually answer the question, you can  generate the vector of occformulas using the rep() function, e.g.

occformulas <- rep("~1", 45)

(Assuming no covariates)

Ken

> Hi Tristan,
>
> Unless you have an absolutely gigantic dataset, you are unlikely to get useful estimates from unmarked for a 9-species model in which you try to estimate all the possible species interactions up to the 9th order. I would suggest constraining the model in some way. You could consider a smaller subset of species (2-4, maybe 5 tends to work well). Emma,

The reason for this error:

Error in pmat[j, not_na] <- ps :
  number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length

turned out to be that the location of missing values did not match for all species across sites. There was at least one site where there was an observation for say, species 1 but the corresponding observation was missing for another species. Unfortunately the model can't handle that scenario properly, either all species have to be non-missing or all have to be missing for a given observation. The solution is to just fill in NAs for all species for any observation where there is any NA for any species.

For example if your observation y-matrices are leopardmat, spottedmat, and lionmat:

any_na <- is.na <http://is.na>(leopardmat) | is.na <http://is.na>(spottedmat) | is.na <http://is.na>(lionmat) #find observations where at least one observation across species is NA
leopardmat[any_na] <- NA #overwrite observations that don't match with NA for each species
spottedmat[any_na] <- NA
lionmat[any_na] <- NA

Then build your y-list and your unmarked frame and everything should work. I'll add a check for this to unmarkedFrameOccuMulti() with an informative warning so that it is handled automatically in the future.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hello everybody,

Sorry for this long email, but I am starting to use MSOMs for analyzing my bird data, and I am struggling how to conceptualize the appropiate model according to my data.

Some background:

I have two main questions that I want to address using MSOMs: (1) how species richness and (2) specific species occupancy probabilities changes along with a moisture gradient and between rainy and dry seasons. My sampling design consists of 12 transects along the gradient - from dry to wet forest - and within each transect, I have 10 point counts (in total 120 point counts). Transects are at least 1.5 km apart, and point counts within a transect are at least 150 m apart. I divided and entire year into four seasons: wet season, wet-dry transition, dry season, and dry-wet transition, according to historical precipitation data. Each point count was visited three times each season. I am assuming occupancy is static at units within seasons but may change between seasons due to seasonal movements of the species.

Preliminary analysis:

For richness, I have previously analyzed my data using the Jackknife estimator for each of the four seasons independently. I pooled all three surveys from point counts into one value and used each of the 10 point counts at the transect level as replicates. As a result, I have a richness estimator at each of the 12 transects per season, using elevation as explanoatory variable (where humid forest is at higher elevation). Species richness is higher at the wet forest in any given sason, and richness is higher in the drier season (dry-wet transition) than in the wet season. Presumably dry forest birds will move in the humid forest during the drier month of the year.

For the species occupancy probabilities, first, I used an implicit dynamic model for each of the species separetly. I fit a single-sepecies single-season model (occu function in unmarked), using the data for all the seasons at once but fitimg separate parameters for every season. I used seasons as a covariate for detection probability and season and elevation as a covariate for occupancy. For most of the species there are differences in occupancy probability along the gradient, and for some species also between seasons, that could be interpretated as seasonal movements. Separetly, for each species, I used an explicit dynamic model (colext function in unmarked)  for modeling local colonization and extintion probabilities between seasons along the gradient, and also used Season for p and Season + elevation for psi, gam and eps. Here is an example of one species:

Doubts and questions about using MSOMs:

1. When modeling species richness, in order to not lose information from the temporal replicates, it will be better if I estimate species richness at the point count (PC) level (instead of at the transect level) using the full DR community occupancy model with data augmentation? I was thinking of treating each transect as a metacommunity and each PC within that transect as a community, and the species that I never detected at a PC level will come (data augmentation) from the total species at the transect level. I cannot use the total number of species occurring in the entire gradient for data augmentation, because some species, according to their climatic preferences, would never be present at some specific locations in the gradient.

2. Can I run a model with all the data together (all the seasons), estimating species richness at each PC, treating each transect as a random effect, and fit separate parameters for every season? Or should I treat seasons as a random effect too?

3. When running the static vs. dynamic models for each species, I am more interested in the differences of occupancy among seasons than estimated probabilities of colonization and extinction between season. If I want to estimate psi at each season using the dynamic model, it will result in too many parameters?, taking into consideration that psi will be a derivated parameter from col and ext probabilities.

4. Should I use the approach from Kery et. al. 2009, for temporary emigration, extending multispecies site-occupancy models for a temporally dynamic situation?

Thanks you for your responses, and I apologize if some of the questions doesn't make sense. I am still learnig about hierarchical modeling.

Saludos,

Diego

messages.subject: Re: occuMulti questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Henry,

1) The "~1" formula represents an intercept-only model (the 1 represents the intercept in R formulas) for the parameter in question, with no covariates. So when you set detFormulas to c('~1', '~1', '~1', '~1') you are specifying that you want to model unique, but constant, detection probabilities for each species. If you aren't interested in covariate effects on detection probability in your models, then yes, this will always remain the same for you.

2) Again, for the formulas on natural parameters, ~1 represents an intercept-only model with no covariates. The "0" or "~0" structure for some natural parameters is a unique feature of occuMulti. To fully understand what each natural parameter is doing in the model I would suggest reading Chris Rota's papers on the model. The short version is that the multispecies occupancy model estimates interaction effects among species. If you have two species in your model it will estimate the pairwise interaction. If you have three species it will measure each of the three pairwise interactions (species 1&2, 1&3, 2&3) and the three-way interaction (species 1&2&3), and so on if you have >3 species. In many cases you may not be interested in these higher-order interactions among species. They require a lot of data to get good estimates and (in my opinion) are often hard to interpret. So, you can tell occuMulti to just not estimate these interactions by specifying "0" or "~0" in the corresponding formula.

Say you had 3 species, just to keep things simpler. Your state formulas should contain 7 formulas: 3 formulas for the single-species occupancy parameters, 3 formulas for the 3 pairwise interactions (1&2, 1&3, 2&3), and one formula for the three-way interaction (1&2&3) in that order. If they were all intercept only with no covariates this would be:

c("~1", "~1", "~1", "~1", "~1", "~1", "~1")

If you decide you didn't want to estimate the three-way interaction term, you would replace the corresponding formula with "~0":

c("~1", "~1", "~1", "~1", "~1", "~1", "~0")

And it would no longer be estimated or appear in the model output.

3) Supplying starting values it not usually necessary, and generally it's better to avoid it. Sometimes if your model does not converge, it can be helpful to supply the starting values, but picking good values can be quite a challenge and is not worth worrying about until you decide it's necessary.

Ken

On Saturday, January 19, 2019 at 7:42:51 AM UTC+11 John Clare wrote:
> Hi Dechen,
>
> Your questions hit on some of the mechanics of maximum likelihood estimation--I'll give this a shot, but there are certainly many other people on the board whom are better equipped to answer.
> The principle behind MLE is that the best guess for a parameter value theta is that value of theta for which pr(data|theta) is greatest. In practice, your computer is using some algorithm to iteratively guess at values of theta until it finds those values where pr(data|theta) is greatest. Sometimes, the computer doesn't quite do as well as one would like. For example, it might explore some wildly incorrect part of the possible parameter space and converge upon some local optima (a combination of values for which the likelihood is greater than nearby combinations of parameter values); it might explore some wildly incorrect part of the possible parameter space where all guesses are extremely and nearly equivalently unlikely and ultimately give up and provide some convergence error. These issues can be more likely to occur if the algorithm starts its sequences of guesses in said bad part of the parameter space, and entering arguments for starting values is one way to make sure the algorithm at least starts its guesses with plausible values. Maybe the easiest way to specify starting values is to look at the the estimates from a similar/nested model using the same data.
> Re. the sequence and specific values used: for a occu model ~1~1, one value corresponds to p on the logit scale, and one to psi on the logit scale because this is the link function used(I don't remember whether detection or occupancy comes first). The inverse logit of 0 or 1 respectively equals 0.5 or about 0.7, for what it's worth: these might or might not be realistic starting values for what you've got.
> The variance covariance matrix and standard errors are derived from the Hessian matrix, which is based on second deriviatives of the likelihood w/ respect to the parameters (if there's a really pronounced maxima w/r/t some parameter, the SE is smaller). If you specify se=FALSE, than the call to occu does not include calculating the Hessian, and so both you avoid any error about it being singular and cannot estimate standard errors
> Calculation of the Hessian is more difficult and can fail when the model is very complex (overfit) or if the optimizer ends up on some ridge in the likelihood, hence the error message.
> As to what is triggering the error with your data...completely speculating, but perhaps p is very low?
>
> Cheers,
>
> John

messages.body_plain:
Alex,

If you are looking for the "mean occupancy" from your model, I think you need to step back a little and consider what you are looking for exactly. If your model has a number of covariates and you find that these covariates influence occupancy, then you should consider whether it is reasonable to get a "mean occupancy" and what it would actually mean. In your example, both elevation (-) and trails (+) influence occupancy: i.e., the model is suggesting that occupancy varies with elevation and trails.

If you consider it sensible to get a "mean occupancy" from a single model, then there would be a number of potential ways of doing so, namely

-running an intercept-only model for occupancy

-computing a prediction of occupancy by inserting the mean of each variable from your data set into the logit equation of occupancy

-computing a prediction of occupancy by inserting the mean of each variable from your study area into the logit equation of occupancy

To help you get further, note that you can find useful information on this forum in already posted threads.

Good luck,

Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Mean Occupancy Estimate from occu()
messages.body_plain:
Alex,

It depends on what the "mean" occupancy is supposed to represent. Here are a few possible options:

1) The expected occupancy probability at a theoretical "average" site with average values for each covariate
You can get this with the predict() function and supplying newdata:

predict(fm6, "state", newdata=data.frame(Elevation=mean(siteCovs(ODVI_umf)$Elevation, Trails=mean(siteCovs(ODVI_umf)$Trails))

2) The mean of the expected occupancies at each actual site
You can also get this with predict(). If you call it without newdata it will give you the expected occupancy probability at each site your dataset:

pr <- predict(fm6, "state")
mean(pr$Predicted)

3) The Empirical Bayes estimate of the "realized" proportion of sites occupied (the estimated mean of the latent occupancy state Z across sites).
You can get this with ranef() and bup().

re <- ranef(fm6)
mean(bup(re, stat="mode"))

See ?ranef and ?bup for more on the last one.

Ken

On Fri, Aug 21, 2020 at 3:41 AM Kery Marc <marc...@vogelwarte.ch> wrote:

> Dear Rachel,
>
> quite a standard sample design, but quite hard to properly analyse and interpret, I would say. Here are a couple of comments:
>
> First of all, the Nmix model of Royle 2004 is probably not appropriate for your data, since it requires that each individual is only counted once. You count tracks, and I presume that it is quite possible that the same hare crosses the line multiple times within a 30m segment, thus violating this basic assumption, producing some sort of a false positive error. If you think that the problem of such multi-counting is quite common, then you *might* experiment with the Poisson-Poisson N-mixture model (see Stanley and Royle 2005, Guillera Arroita et al. 2011; also Section 6.13.2 in the AHM1 book), which does allow an individual to appear in a count multiple times. However, my own experience with this model is rather negative: it yielded what were deemed to be unrealistic estimates and I concluded that it is probably very sensitive to subtle violations of the parametric assumptions. Though of course in other situations it might perform OK.
>
> If however you are quite confident that a hare can only be counted once per 30-m segment or perhaps if you actually follow their tracks and make sure that you only count once the hare with a track that crosses the line multiple times, then you should be fine in principle with the basic Nmix model.
>
> If you can't exclude multiple counts and don't want to use the Poisson/Poisson Nmix model, then one of your usual fall-back positions would be some sort of Poisson GLMM, where you merely model intensity of use, which is the combination of abundance and detection rate that the Nmix models attempt to separate out. In GLMMs, it would be simple to account for non-independence of counts for 30-m segments within the same transect, either with or without spatial autocorrelation.
>
> You could also account for spatial autocorrelation inside of an Nmix model; see Aing et al., JAPPL, 2011 (which is for an occupancy model, but for linear data along transects, and you could do the same thing also inside of an Nmix model). See Chapter 9 in our upcoming AHM2 book (very soon now !)
>
